hook: When a lava flow cools on Hawaii, it leaves black rock with no soil and no life. Within a few years, lichens and ferns appear in the cracks. A farm field abandoned in New England tells a faster story: weeds the first summer, shrubs within a decade, a young forest within a few decades. Both are ecological succession; what differs is whether soil was there to start with.

prereq.q: How is a disruption that recurs at irregular intervals, such as wildfire in many forests, classified?
prereq.why: Recurring, but not at regular intervals, is episodic.
Richness is the count of species.

figure.caption: Primary succession starts on bare rock with no soil; secondary succession starts where soil remains after a disruption. Both move toward a mature community.

chain.cause: A disruption leaves bare rock (primary) or bare soil (secondary)
chain.effect: pioneer species, which grow fast and spread easily, arrive first

chain.cause: Pioneers change the site: they help make soil, add nutrients and give shade
chain.effect: conditions become suitable for larger plants that could not grow there before

chain.cause: Larger, longer-lived plants arrive and outcompete the pioneers
chain.effect: the community changes in stages, and species richness and biomass increase

chain.cause: Many years pass without a major disruption
chain.effect: a mature, more stable community (climax community) develops

ideas: Ecological succession is the gradual change in the species of a community after a disruption, in a series of stages.
Primary succession starts where there is no soil: new lava rock, rock left by a retreating glacier. Soil must form first, so it is slow (often centuries).
Secondary succession starts where soil remains after a disruption such as a fire, a flood, a hurricane or an abandoned farm field. With soil and seeds already present, it is faster (often decades).
Pioneer species (lichens and mosses on rock; grasses and weeds on soil) arrive first. Over time biodiversity and biomass increase, and a mature, more stable climax community develops.

misconception.wrong: Succession after a forest fire is primary succession, because almost everything was burned.
misconception.right: A fire leaves soil, and usually seeds and roots in it, so regrowth after a fire is secondary succession. Primary succession needs a start with no soil at all, such as new rock.

summary: Ecological succession is the series of changes in a community after a disruption. Primary succession begins on bare rock with no soil, and pioneer species such as lichens and mosses help form soil; it is slow. Secondary succession begins where soil remains, after a fire, flood or abandoned farm; it is faster. Over the stages, biodiversity and biomass increase until a mature, more stable climax community develops.
